etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 至 ‘to arrive’ + phonetic 刀.

funFacts: 到！ is what Chinese pupils answer at roll call — ‘present!’ (‘arrived’).
pitfalls: ‘Go to school’ is simply 我去学校: the verb 去 already contains the ‘to’, no extra word is needed.
到 + place + verb means ‘go to … to do …’: 到超市买牛奶. The place comes BEFORE the action, the order in which things happen.
subtleties: 到学校 stresses reaching the place; 去学校 tells where you are heading.
At the start of a phone call 我到了 means ‘I’m here, I’ve arrived’.
‘Arrive’ takes the place directly: 到北京 ‘arrive in Beijing’ — no ‘in’ word; ‘until’ follows the verb: 工作到六点 ‘work until six’, 从早到晚 ‘from morning till night’.

etymology.text: Originally written 从, two people one behind the other (‘to follow’); the traditional 從 adds 辵 ‘walk’. The simplified form went back to the original.

funFacts: The simplified 从 is older than the traditional 從: it was the original drawing of one person following another.
pitfalls: 从 + place stands before the verb: 我从家来 — not *我来从家.
‘Where are you from?’ (origin) is 你是哪里人？; 从 is for where someone or something comes from now: 你从哪里来？
subtleties: 从…到… works for place and time: 从家到学校, 从早到晚 ‘from morning till night’.
For distance Chinese uses 离, not 从: 超市离我家很近 (S12).

pitfalls: 跟 + person + 一起 + verb: 我跟他一起吃饭 — the verb comes last; *我吃饭跟他 is wrong.
跟 is ‘with’ for people only. ‘With chopsticks’ is 用筷子 (用 ‘to use’), ‘coffee with milk’ 加牛奶的咖啡 (加 ‘to add’).
subtleties: 跟 is the everyday spoken ‘with’ in the north; 和 is more neutral; writing uses 与.

etymology.text: Simplified from 爲. In the oracle-bone script a hand leading an elephant — ‘to do, to make’; wèi ‘for’ is a derivative of wéi ‘to do, to be’.

funFacts: The oldest form of 为 shows a hand leading an elephant.

subtleties: 为 sounds more formal than 给: in speech 妈妈给我们做饭; 为 for causes and toasts: 为人民服务, 为…干杯.

subtleties: The 一 is said yì before 起 (yìqǐ), by the tone rule of 一.

pitfalls: 车站 is a bus or train station, or a stop; a metro station is 地铁站.
subtleties: 站 also means ‘to stand’: 站在门口 ‘to stand at the door’.

kōnggǎng: airport (in names)

etymology.text: Short for 飞机场 ‘aeroplane field’ (飞机 ‘flying machine’ + 场 ‘field’).

funFacts: 飞机 ‘aeroplane’ is a ‘flying machine’, so 机场 is the ‘machine field’ for short.
pitfalls: 机场 jīchǎng and 鸡场 jīchǎng ‘chicken farm’ sound the same — the characters tell them apart.
subtleties: In slang 机场 is a provider of tools to get round internet censorship (from a paper-plane logo).

mǎlù: road, street (for traffic)
hútòng: lane, alley (Beijing)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 行 ‘road’ + phonetic 圭. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *r/g-wa ‘village’.

funFacts: The character 街 is 行 ‘road’ opened in the middle to hold 圭 — the street running between.
pitfalls: ‘In the street’ takes 上 (S12): 在街上.
subtleties: 逛街 ‘to stroll the streets’ means going shopping.

synonyms.nuance: gòuwù zhōngxīn: shopping centre — 广场 in names often means this

etymology.text: Borrowed in writing from Japanese 広場 hiroba ‘open place’.

funFacts: 广场舞 ‘square dancing’: in the evening groups of (mostly retired) people dance to music in squares all over China.
pitfalls: In a name, 广场 is often a shopping centre, not an open square.
subtleties: ‘In the square’ is 在广场上, with 上 (S12).

At the weekend we go to the park.

synonyms.nuance: huāyuán: garden (also a small park)
yuán: garden, park — in names: 动物园 ‘zoo’

etymology.text: 公 ‘public’ + 园 ‘garden’ (semantic 囗 ‘enclosure’ + phonetic 袁).

funFacts: 园 ‘garden’ makes 动物园 ‘animal garden’ (zoo) and 幼儿园 ‘little children’s garden’ — a kindergarten, as in German Kindergarten.
pitfalls: 在公园 and 在公园里 are both fine; 里 stresses ‘inside the park’.
subtleties: 公 ‘public’ is also in 公共汽车 ‘bus’ and 公司 ‘company’.

dūshì: metropolis

etymology.text: 城 ‘city wall’ (semantic 土 ‘earth’ — walls of stamped earth) + 市 ‘market’.

funFacts: 城 first meant the city wall of stamped earth; 长城 ‘the long wall’ is the Great Wall.
pitfalls: In names ‘city’ is 市: 北京市; 城市 is the general noun.
subtleties: 座 is the elegant measure word for cities: 一座城市.

nóngcūn: the countryside, rural areas
xiāngxia: the country, one’s rural home
cūnzhuāng: village (written)

etymology.text: 村 (semantic 木 ‘tree’ + phonetic 寸) + the noun suffix 子.

funFacts: Villages are often named after a family: 王家村 ‘the Wangs’ village’.
pitfalls: ‘In the village’ is 在村子里 — 村子 is an ordinary noun and takes 里 (S12).
subtleties: 农村 is the countryside as opposed to the city; 村子 is one village.

zǔguó: the motherland (emotional)

etymology.text: In ancient China the fief of a feudal lord was a 国 and that of a minister a 家; together they came to mean ‘country, state’.

funFacts: 国家 joins the old words for a lord’s fief (国) and a minister’s (家).
pitfalls: ‘Which country are you from?’ is 你是哪国人？ (哪 + 国 + 人).
subtleties: 国家 is the state or nation; ‘the country(side)’ is 农村.

part from — written, mostly in compounds (离家, 离婚)

senses.def: from (for distance): A 离 B 很近 / 很远

etymology.text: Traditional 離: phonetic 离 + semantic 隹 ‘bird’ — first the name of a bird (the oriole), borrowed for ‘to leave, to part’.

funFacts: 離 first named a bird, the black-naped oriole; the meaning ‘to part’ is a sound loan.
pitfalls: Distance takes 离, not 从: 我家离学校很近 — *我家从学校很近 is wrong.
subtleties: 离 also counts time: 离春节还有三天 ‘three days to go until the Spring Festival’.

absent.reason: Chinese has no preposition ‘in’. 在 (known since S01) + a place says where something is: 在学校 ‘at / in school’, 在北京 ‘in Beijing’. An ordinary noun becomes a place with 里 ‘inside’ after it (S12): 在房间里 ‘in the room’.
absent.use: 在 + place noun (学校, 医院, 超市 …) or 在 + noun + 里: 我在家; 牛奶在冰箱里

absent.reason: Chinese has no separate ‘at’: 在 (known since S01) + place does the job — 在家 ‘at home’, 在学校 ‘at school’, 在车站 ‘at the station’. Greek σε, English at / in and German in / an / bei all become 在.
absent.use: 在 + place, before the verb: 我在银行工作 ‘I work at a bank’

absent.reason: There is no everyday preposition ‘without’: Chinese negates — 没有 ‘there is no / not having’ (没 S08 + 有 S06) + noun, or 不 + a verb such as 要 / 加 ‘add’.
absent.use: 没有 + noun: 没有糖的咖啡 ‘coffee without sugar’, 没有你，我… ‘without you, I…’; 不 + verb: 我喝咖啡不要糖 ‘I take coffee without sugar’; written 无: 无糖 ‘sugar-free’
